title: Troubleshooting
text: When a Positron session does not start, the cause is almost always in one of three places: the install on the compute node, the license file, or the OOD reverse proxy. This page is organized by symptom. Each section says where to look and what the log shows.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Where to look first
Every session has an output directory under the user’s home directory:
~/ondemand/data/sys/dashboard/batch_connect/sys/positron/output/<session-id>/
The Session ID link on the session card opens this directory in the OOD file browser. output.log holds everything the job printed, including the messages from positron-server. The directory also keeps the rendered script.sh and before.sh, and job_script_options.json with the Slurm options that OOD submitted.
A healthy start looks like this:
Script starting...
Wed Oct 14 20:35:05 UTC 2026: Waiting for Positron Server to open port 25184...
TIMING - Starting main script at: Wed Oct 14 20:35:05 UTC 2026
Wed Oct 14 20:35:05 UTC 2026: Running on cpn01:25184
TIMING - Starting positron-server at: Wed Oct 14 20:35:05 UTC 2026
Server bound to 0.0.0.0:25184 (IPv4)
Extension host agent listening on 25184

Positron license verified: {"status":"activated", ...}
Verified license from license-manager directory.
Wed Oct 14 20:35:05 UTC 2026: Positron Server is listening on port 25184
After that, positron-server logs the extensions it unpacks on a first start, then Extension host agent started. Messages about vsda.js and vsda_bg.wasm not found are normal.
Errors in the form itself, before a job is submitted, go to the OOD per-user log on the OOD host:


Terminal

tail -50 /var/log/ondemand-nginx/<username>/error.log

title: Troubleshooting
section: The Positron tile does not appear
text:
The Positron tile does not appear

The app directory has the wrong name or location. OOD lists every directory under /var/www/ood/apps/sys/ that has a manifest.yml. Confirm /var/www/ood/apps/sys/positron/manifest.yml exists.
cluster in form.yml does not match a cluster file. OOD hides an app whose cluster is not defined. The value must match a file name in /etc/ood/config/clusters.d/, without .yml.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
The form shows a 500 error
form.yml did not parse. Check the per-user log on the OOD host for the line that names the problem, then fix the YAML. A common cause is a value with a colon or a quote that is not quoted.

title: Troubleshooting
section: The session stays in Starting, then disappears
text:
The session stays in Starting, then disappears
positron-server exited before it opened the port, or right after. The session card can show Running for a moment, because the server opens the port before it checks the license. Open output.log and find the last message from positron-server. The sections below cover the messages you can see.
With this app, after.sh stops the job as soon as positron-server exits, so the card goes away within a few seconds. On a job that stays in Starting for the full 10 minutes, the server is running but the port never opened. See The port never opens.

positron-server: command not found
The job did not find the server. The job runs on the compute node that the session card names, with a login shell, so the OOD host’s PATH and the shell you tested in do not count. Check, in this order:

positron_server_dir in form.yml is the directory that contains bin/positron-server. On the compute node from the session card, run ls <positron_server_dir>/bin. An install that exists on the OOD host or the login node but not on the compute node fails exactly this way.
If you use a module, positron_module names a module that exists on the compute nodes, and the module adds bin to PATH. The rendered script.sh in the session directory shows the exact module load line.
The compute node can run the binary. On the node, run /opt/positron-server/bin/positron-server --version.



script.sh: Permission denied
template/script.sh.erb lost its execute bit, usually after a copy that did not keep file modes. On the OOD host, run:


Terminal

chmod +x /var/www/ood/apps/sys/positron/template/script.sh.erb

title: Troubleshooting
text:
License errors
positron-server validates the license before it accepts connections. It looks for license.lic in its activation directory, <install>/resources/activation/linux/<arch>/, and runs the bundled license-manager to check it. Check the license on a compute node first:


Terminal

/opt/positron-server/resources/activation/linux/<arch>/license-manager status


No license key provided
No license key provided. A license key is required to use Positron in a hosted
environment. Provide a license key with the --license-key or --license-key-file
command-line arguments, or set the POSITRON_LICENSE_KEY or
POSITRON_LICENSE_KEY_FILE environment variables.
Do not follow the advice in the message. It appears whenever positron-server finds no usable license, and the command-line options it names are for signed per-session keys that this app does not use. Check:

The file is missing. ls the activation directory on a compute node. The file name must end in .lic.
The file is in the wrong architecture directory. positron-server reads linux/x86_64 on x86_64 nodes and linux/aarch64 on ARM64 nodes. Both directories ship in every archive. uname -m on the node tells you which one it reads.
The install directory is not mounted on the compute node. The install can be visible on the OOD host and absent on the node.



libcrypto.so.3 or GLIBC_2.34 not found
license-manager: error while loading shared libraries: libcrypto.so.3:
cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
license-manager: /lib64/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.34' not found
The bundled license-manager links against OpenSSL 3 and glibc 2.34. The compute node runs an older release, so every license check fails and the session log shows No license key provided. positron-server itself needs only glibc 2.28, so the server starts, binds the port, and then exits. Run the sessions on nodes with RHEL 9, Rocky Linux 9, Ubuntu 22.04, or a newer release. RHEL 8 and Rocky Linux 8 do not meet the glibc requirement, and a newer OpenSSL package alone does not fix it.


The license file next to the license-manager binary was rejected
The file exists but license-manager did not accept it. The rest of the line names the reason:

Permission denied: each session reads the file as the user who launched it, so a root-only mode such as 600 fails every session. Set the mode to 644.
License has expired: ask Posit for a replacement file.
Invalid license result or a signature error: the file was altered, or it is not a Positron Server license. Copy the file again from the original you received from Posit.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
The port never opens
The session stays in Starting for 10 minutes, then disappears, and output.log ends with:
Timed out waiting for Positron Server to open port 25184
after.sh checks the port from the compute node itself, so a firewall is not the cause here. The server is running but slow. The usual reasons:

The first start for a user. positron-server unpacks its built-in extensions into ~/.positron-server the first time. On a slow home filesystem this can take several minutes. Later starts are faster.
Too little memory. Look for oom-kill in output.log or in the Slurm job record with sacct -j <jobid> -o State,MaxRSS. Raise the memory request. Positron Server needs at least 2.5 GB.
shuf, ss, and lsof are all missing on the node. OOD uses them to find and check the port. after.sh cannot see the port without one of them. Install iproute for ss.

To give slow nodes more time, raise the 600 in template/after.sh.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Connect to Positron shows an error or a blank page
text:
Connect to Positron shows an error or a blank page
The session is Running, but the new tab does not show Positron.

OOD shows “Not Found” or its own 404 page. The /rnode/ reverse proxy is off. Set rnode_uri: "/rnode" in /etc/ood/config/ood_portal.yml, run update_ood_portal, and restart Apache. See Turn on the reverse proxy.
OOD shows “Proxy Error” or a 502. The OOD host could not reach the compute node on the session port. Either the session ended, or a firewall blocks the port range between the OOD host and the compute nodes. From the OOD host, run curl -s http://<node>:<port>/ with the values from the session card. OOD picks a port between 2000 and 65535 by default.
The host name is rejected. host_regex in ood_portal.yml does not match the node name that the session card shows. Change the pattern so it matches every compute node.
The tab shows 403 Forbidden. Positron Server did not get a token it accepts. If a user copied the address without the tkn parameter, or the token cookie expired, the Connect to Positron button fixes it. If the button itself lands on Forbidden, the token did not reach one side. In the session directory, connection.yml must have a password line and connection-token must hold the same value. An empty password means before.sh did not run, usually because an edit to template/before.sh.erb broke it, and the rendered before.sh in the session directory shows what ran.
The tab stays blank with no error. The browser blocked the pop-up, or the page is still loading its assets through the proxy. Allow pop-ups for the OOD host and reload the tab.

title: Troubleshooting
section: R or Python does not appear in the console
text:
R or Python does not appear in the console
Positron finds interpreters on the PATH of the server process, and in the usual install locations. The session has the PATH of a login shell on the compute node, plus positron_server_dir/bin. Load the R and Python modules you want in template/script.sh.erb, before the server starts, or install them in a location Positron scans, such as /usr/bin or /opt/R.
Python also needs the ipykernel package. Positron ships a bundled copy and uses it when the interpreter has none.
The interpreter picker shows Discovering interpreters… while Positron looks for R and Python. The R extension writes what it found, and why it rejected an install, to a log under the user’s home directory on the compute node:
~/.local/state/positron/logs/<timestamp>/exthost*/positron.positron-r/R Language Pack.log
A log with no Candidate R binary line means discovery did not run. A Filtering out line names the install and the reason, such as a version below the minimum Positron supports.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Slow start

A first session for a user takes longer. See The port never opens.
Sessions on a busy partition wait in Queued until Slurm has a node. squeue -u <username> shows the reason.
Inside Apptainer, the first start also unpacks the image. Put the .sif file on a fast local or parallel filesystem, not on NFS over a slow link.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Still stuck?
Open an issue at the positron-server-ood issue tracker with output.log from the session directory, your Positron Server version, your OOD version, and the operating system of the compute nodes.

title: positron-server-ood
text: Run Positron Server on an HPC cluster through Open OnDemand (OOD).

title: positron-server-ood
text:
Overview
positron-server-ood is an OOD interactive app. It adds a Positron tile to the OOD dashboard. When a user launches it, OOD submits a Slurm job that starts Positron Server on a compute node, and the user reaches the full Positron IDE in the browser through the OOD reverse proxy. Users need no local install.
Positron is a data science IDE built on Code OSS, with:

Rich Python and R support
A console, variables pane, data explorer, and plot viewer
An integrated debugger, help pane, and version control
Access to the OpenVSX extension marketplace

title: positron-server-ood
text:
Requirements

Open OnDemand 3.0 or newer, with a Slurm cluster and the /rnode/ reverse proxy enabled
Positron Server 2026.10.0-297 or newer, installed where the compute nodes can read it
A Positron Server license file from Posit. Positron Server refuses to start in a hosted environment without one, and Get started shows where it goes
Compute nodes with glibc 2.34 or newer and OpenSSL 3, such as RHEL 9 or Ubuntu 22.04
At least 2.5 GB of RAM per session. See Memory

title: positron-server-ood
text:
Where to start



Page
Use it to




Get started
Install Positron Server, place the license, install the app, and launch a session.


Configuration
Change form fields and site settings, run inside Apptainer, use GPUs, add bind mounts.


Troubleshooting
Find out why a session does not start.


Test checklist
Run through the features after install and report the results.

title: Configuration
text: You configure the app in two files. form.yml holds the site settings and the form fields that users see. submit.yml.erb turns the form values into Slurm options. The scripts under template/ start Positron Server on the compute node. This page covers each setting, then the Apptainer, GPU, and license options.

title: Configuration
text:
Site settings
The site settings are the fixed values at the top of form.yml. Users do not see them. Each one is a string. An empty string turns the setting off.



Setting
Default
Description




cluster
"hpc"
The cluster the job is submitted to. It must match a file name in /etc/ood/config/clusters.d/, without .yml. The default matches the local validation cluster.


positron_server_dir
"/opt/positron-server"
Directory of a plain Positron Server install. The job adds <positron_server_dir>/bin to PATH. Leave it empty when positron-server is already on PATH, or when the module below provides it.


positron_module
""
An environment module to load before the server starts, for example positron-server/2026.10.0. The job runs module load with this value.


apptainer_image
""
Path to an Apptainer image. When set, the job runs positron-server inside this image. See Run inside Apptainer.


apptainer_binds
""
Extra bind mounts for Apptainer, comma separated, for example /scratch,/project. Only used when apptainer_image is set.




Install location
The job finds positron-server in this order:

If positron_module is set, the job loads that module.
If positron_server_dir is set, the job puts <positron_server_dir>/bin first on PATH.
The job runs positron-server from PATH.

So a site with a module sets positron_module and leaves positron_server_dir empty. A site with a shared directory sets positron_server_dir. A site that already has positron-server on every user’s PATH leaves both empty.

title: Configuration
text:
Form fields
These are the fields that users see when they launch the app. To change a default, edit the value of the field in form.yml. To hide a field and fix its value, replace the whole field entry with a string, for example num_gpus: "0".



Field
Label
Default
Description




working_dir
Working directory
user’s home
The directory Positron opens. The user picks it with the OOD file picker. A path that does not exist falls back to the home directory.


bc_account
Account
none
Slurm account, passed as --account. With no value, OOD omits the option and Slurm uses the user’s default account.


bc_queue
Partition
none
Slurm partition, passed as --partition. With no value, OOD omits the option and Slurm uses the default partition.


bc_num_hours
Hours
1
Wall time in hours. OOD passes it as --time.


num_cores
Cores
1
CPU cores. Passed as --cpus-per-task.


memory_gb
Memory (GB)
2.5
Memory for the job, in GB. Passed as --mem in MB. Positron Server needs at least 2.5 GB.


num_gpus
GPUs
0
Number of GPUs. When above 0, the job adds --gres=gpu:<n>. See GPUs.



bc_account, bc_queue, and bc_num_hours are OOD built-in fields. OOD turns them into Slurm options itself, and leaves the option out of the job when the field is blank. The native list in submit.yml.erb adds the rest:


submit.yml.erb

script:
  native:
    - "--nodes=1"
    - "--ntasks=1"
    - "--cpus-per-task=<%= num_cores.blank? ? 1 : num_cores.to_i %>"
    - "--mem=<%= ((memory_gb.blank? ? 2.5 : memory_gb.to_f) * 1024).round %>M"
<%- if num_gpus.to_i > 0 -%>
    - "--gres=gpu:<%= num_gpus.to_i %>"
<%- end -%>

Add your own Slurm options to this list. For example, to make every session use a QOS, add - "--qos=interactive".

Memory
Allocate memory per session based on the size of the workload:








Workload
Minimum
Recommended




Light: one console, a few extensions, simple scripts
2 GB
2.5 GB


Standard: several consoles, several extensions, app development
2.5 GB
4 GB


Heavy: large datasets, language servers, several apps at once
4 GB
6 GB or more



Slurm stops a session that goes over the request. Signs of too little memory are slow runtime switching, extensions that fail to install, and crashes during large operations.

title: Configuration
text:
Template variables
The scripts in template/ read the form values through context. They also set these variables:








Variable
Set in
Description




port
before.sh.erb
A free port on the compute node, from the OOD find_port helper.


password
before.sh.erb
A random 32-character connection token. OOD writes it to the session’s connection.yml, and the Connect button sends it as the tkn query parameter.


POSITRON_CONNECTION_TOKEN_FILE
before.sh.erb
Path of the token file, connection-token in the session’s output directory, mode 600. Passed to positron-server as --connection-token-file.



script.sh.erb starts the server with these options:


template/script.sh.erb

positron-server \
  --host "0.0.0.0" \
  --port "${port}" \
  --connection-token-file "${POSITRON_CONNECTION_TOKEN_FILE}" \
  --accept-server-license-terms \
  --telemetry-level off \
  --disable-workspace-trust \
  --default-folder "<working_dir>"

--disable-workspace-trust turns off the Code OSS workspace trust prompt. Without it, Positron opens the working directory in Restricted Mode and refuses to start a console until the user selects Trust this folder. The user picked the directory and owns the session, so the prompt adds nothing. Remove the option from script.sh.erb to bring the prompt back.
The server keeps its data in ~/.positron-server for each user. Extensions and settings persist from one session to the next.
after.sh waits up to 600 seconds for the port to open. Raise that number if your compute nodes are slow to start a job.

title: Configuration
text:
Run inside Apptainer
Many HPC sites run interactive apps from an Apptainer image rather than from a host install, so that the compute nodes need nothing beyond Apptainer. This app supports that. The steps are:

Build an image that contains Positron Server, the license file, and the R and Python installs that users need. The example definition file below is a starting point.
Put the .sif file on a filesystem that every compute node mounts.
Check the image on a compute node:


Terminal

apptainer exec positron-server.sif positron-server --version
apptainer exec positron-server.sif \
  /opt/positron-server/resources/activation/linux/<arch>/license-manager status

Set apptainer_image in form.yml to the path of the .sif file. Leave positron_server_dir at /opt/positron-server if that is where the image keeps the install, or empty if the image puts positron-server on PATH.

With apptainer_image set, the job runs:


template/script.sh.erb

apptainer exec --bind "${BINDS}" "<apptainer_image>" positron-server ...

BINDS is the session output directory, TMPDIR when it is set, and the value of apptainer_binds. Apptainer binds the home directory by default. Add any other filesystem the user needs, such as scratch or project space, to apptainer_binds.
The image must have positron-server on PATH, or positron_server_dir must point at the install inside the image. The job passes positron_server_dir/bin to Apptainer through APPTAINERENV_PREPEND_PATH.
This is an example definition file that unpacks the CDN archive and places the license file. Replace <arch> with x86_64 or aarch64, and put license.lic next to the definition file before you build.


positron-server.def

Bootstrap: docker
From: rockylinux/rockylinux:9

%files
    license.lic /opt/license.lic

%post
    dnf install -y tar gzip
    mkdir -p /opt/positron-server
    CDN=https://cdn.posit.co/positron/releases/server
    curl -L "$CDN/x86_64/positron-server-linux-x64-2026.10.0-297.tar.gz" \
      | tar -xz -C /opt/positron-server --strip-components=1
    install -m 644 /opt/license.lic \
      /opt/positron-server/resources/activation/linux/<arch>/license.lic
    rm /opt/license.lic

%environment
    export PATH=/opt/positron-server/bin:$PATH

Build it with apptainer build positron-server.sif positron-server.def. Install R and Python into the image as well, or bind them in from the host, because the consoles inside Positron use the interpreters that the server process can see.






Note



Confirm with Posit whether your Positron Server build should run inside a container. The example definition is untested against a production site, and the command and bind list are the only parts this app controls.

title: Configuration
text:
GPUs
When a user requests one or more GPUs:

submit.yml.erb adds --gres=gpu:<n> to the Slurm job.
With Apptainer, script.sh.erb adds --nv to apptainer exec, so the NVIDIA driver and libraries from the host are visible inside the image.

Positron Server itself does not use a GPU. The GPU is for the R and Python code that users run in the session. If your cluster has no GPUs, hide the field by setting num_gpus: "0" in form.yml.

title: Configuration
text:
License file location
positron-server looks for a license in this order and uses the first one that validates:

The --license-key and --license-key-file command-line options.
The POSITRON_LICENSE_KEY and POSITRON_LICENSE_KEY_FILE environment variables.
A license-key file in the user data directory.
A .lic file in the activation directory, <install>/resources/activation/linux/<arch>/.

The app sets none of the first three. They take a signed per-session key, which a product such as Posit Workbench mints, and on Positron Server 2026.09.0 and newer they also take a raw license.lic. The license file from Posit goes in the activation directory, item 4, as Get started describes. That needs no change to the app and works on a read-only install.






ImportantEvery session user can read the license file



Each session runs positron-server as the user who launched it, and the server reads the license file itself. So the file must be readable by every user who can start a session, wherever you put it, and any of those users can copy it. If that is not acceptable at your site, the alternative is a service that mints a signed per-session key, item 1 or 2 above, from a signing key that users cannot read. Positron Server Pro and Posit Workbench license sessions this way. Setting up such a service is outside this guide. Ask Posit about it when you discuss your license.


If you would rather keep the license file somewhere else, you have two options:

With Apptainer, bind the file to the exact path inside the image. Add /path/to/license.lic:/opt/positron-server/resources/activation/linux/<arch>/license.lic:ro to apptainer_binds. This also works on a read-only install.
Without Apptainer, pass the file to the server. Add --license-key-file "/path/to/license.lic" to POSITRON_ARGS in script.sh.erb, or export POSITRON_LICENSE_KEY_FILE before the server starts. The server copies the file into the activation directory, so the directory must be writable by the first session that starts, and later sessions use the copy.

title: Configuration
text:
Next steps

Troubleshooting covers a session that does not start.
Test checklist is the list to run and report against.

title: Get started
text:
This guide installs Positron Server on an HPC cluster and adds a Positron tile to Open OnDemand (OOD). You do four things: install Positron Server where the compute nodes can read it, place the license file, install this app on the OOD host, and check that the OOD reverse proxy is on. Then you launch a session and run the test checklist.
The guide installs Positron Server directly on a shared filesystem, which is the shortest path to a first session. If your site runs interactive apps from Apptainer images, do Steps 1 and 2 inside an image instead, then continue with Step 3. Run inside Apptainer covers the image.

title: Get started
text:
Before you start
You need:

An OOD host on OOD 3.0 or newer, with a Slurm cluster defined in /etc/ood/config/clusters.d/. The app uses Slurm sbatch options.
Root access on the OOD host, and write access to a filesystem that every compute node mounts, such as /opt or an applications directory.
A Positron Server license file (license.lic) from Posit. Positron Server refuses to start in a hosted environment without a license.
At least 2.5 GB of RAM per session on the compute nodes.
Compute nodes with glibc 2.34 or newer and OpenSSL 3, for example RHEL 9, Rocky Linux 9, or Ubuntu 22.04 or newer. The license-manager binary that checks the license file needs both.

The compute nodes also need the shuf command and ss or lsof, which OOD uses to find a free port. Standard Linux distributions have them.

title: Get started
text:
Step 1: Install Positron Server
Positron Server is available only as a Linux archive from the Posit content delivery network (CDN). It does not appear on the Positron download page or on the GitHub releases page. Download the build that matches the CPU architecture of your compute nodes:



Architecture
Download




x86_64 (Intel and AMD)
positron-server-linux-x64-2026.10.0-297.tar.gz


ARM64
positron-server-linux-arm64-2026.10.0-297.tar.gz



Unpack it into a directory that every compute node can read. This guide uses /opt/positron-server. To download and unpack from the command line, run the commands for your architecture as root, on a host that mounts that directory.
For x86_64:


Terminal

CDN=https://cdn.posit.co/positron/releases/server
curl -L -o /tmp/positron-server.tar.gz \
  "$CDN/x86_64/positron-server-linux-x64-2026.10.0-297.tar.gz"
mkdir -p /opt/positron-server
tar -xzf /tmp/positron-server.tar.gz -C /opt/positron-server \
  --strip-components=1

For ARM64:


Terminal

CDN=https://cdn.posit.co/positron/releases/server
curl -L -o /tmp/positron-server.tar.gz \
  "$CDN/arm64/positron-server-linux-arm64-2026.10.0-297.tar.gz"
mkdir -p /opt/positron-server
tar -xzf /tmp/positron-server.tar.gz -C /opt/positron-server \
  --strip-components=1

Confirm the install from a compute node, not from the OOD host:


Terminal

/opt/positron-server/bin/positron-server --version

In Step 3 you tell the app where this directory is. If your site provides software through environment modules, you can make a module for Positron Server and name that module in Step 3 instead. See Install location.

title: Get started
text:
Step 2: Place the license file
Posit sends the license file to you directly. It is a small text file that starts with -----BEGIN RSTUDIO LICENSE-----, and its name varies.
Copy it into the activation directory, next to the bundled license-manager binary, with the name license.lic. In the command below, replace /path/to/your-license.lic with the file you received, and <arch> with x86_64 or aarch64:


Terminal

install -m 644 /path/to/your-license.lic \
  /opt/positron-server/resources/activation/linux/<arch>/license.lic

The license file needs mode 644. Each session runs positron-server as the user who launched it, and positron-server reads the license file itself. With a root-only mode such as 600, every session fails to start. This also means that every user who can start a session can read the file. See License file location for what that implies and for the alternative.
Before you continue, confirm that license-manager accepts the license file. Run this on a compute node, or on any host with the same architecture:


Terminal

/opt/positron-server/resources/activation/linux/<arch>/license-manager status

The output reports activated or evaluation and the days left. If the install directory is read-only, or several clusters share one install, see License file location for other places to put the file.

title: Get started
text:
Step 3: Install the app
On the OOD host, clone this repository into the system apps directory:


Terminal

cd /var/www/ood/apps/sys
git clone https://github.com/posit-dev/positron-server-ood.git positron

Then open /var/www/ood/apps/sys/positron/form.yml and set the site settings at the top of the file:


form.yml

cluster: "hpc"

attributes:
  positron_server_dir: "/opt/positron-server"
  positron_module: ""
  apptainer_image: ""
  apptainer_binds: ""


cluster is the file name, without .yml, of your cluster in /etc/ood/config/clusters.d/.
positron_server_dir is the directory from Step 1. Leave it empty if positron-server is already on PATH on the compute nodes.
Leave the other three empty for a plain install. Configuration describes them.

OOD reads the app directory on each request. You do not restart anything after you install or edit the app.

title: Get started
section: Step 4: Turn on the reverse proxy
text:
Step 4: Turn on the reverse proxy
OOD connects the browser to the session through its reverse proxy. The app uses the /rnode/ path, which is off by default. In /etc/ood/config/ood_portal.yml, set:


/etc/ood/config/ood_portal.yml

rnode_uri: "/rnode"
host_regex: "[\\w.-]+\\.example\\.com"

Set host_regex to a pattern that matches the host names of your compute nodes, as reported by hostname on the node. Then regenerate the portal configuration and restart Apache:


Terminal

/opt/ood/ood-portal-generator/sbin/update_ood_portal
systemctl restart httpd

Skip this step if rnode_uri is already set. The Jupyter and RStudio apps from the OOD documentation use the same setting.

title: Get started
text:
Step 5: Launch a session

Sign in to OOD and open Interactive Apps, then Positron.
Leave the form at its defaults for the first session. The default request is one core, 2.5 GB of memory, and one hour.
Select Launch. OOD submits a Slurm job and shows the session card under My Interactive Sessions.
When the card changes to Running, select Connect to Positron. Positron opens in a new tab.

The first start takes longer than later starts, because Positron Server unpacks its built-in extensions into ~/.positron-server for that user.

title: Get started
text:
Step 6: Confirm it works
Run the test checklist. It covers the R console, the Python console, files, plots, the data explorer, and a clean session end.

title: Get started
text:
How it works
When a user selects Launch, OOD submits a Slurm job with the resources from the form. On the compute node, the job:

Picks a free port and makes a random connection token.
Loads the module or adds positron_server_dir/bin to PATH.
Starts positron-server on that port with the token file, the license terms accepted, and telemetry off.
Waits up to 10 minutes for the port to open, then marks the session as running.

The Connect to Positron button opens /rnode/<host>/<port>/?tkn=<token>. OOD proxies the request to the compute node, and Positron Server checks the token on every request. Only the user who owns the session has the token.
Positron Server checks the license before it listens on the port. A missing, expired, or altered license stops the session, and OOD reports a timeout. Troubleshooting shows what each failure looks like in the session log.

title: Get started
text:
Next steps

Configuration covers every form field and site setting, Apptainer, GPUs, and extra bind mounts.
Troubleshooting covers a session that does not start.
Test checklist is the list to run and report against.

title: Test checklist
text:
Run this list after you install the app. Each item has a step and an expected result. Record pass or fail for each item, and attach the session log for any failure. Troubleshooting explains where the log is.
Use a normal user account, not root. Use a cluster node with R and Python installed, with the Python ipykernel package available to that Python.

title: Test checklist
text:
1. Launch
Step: Open Interactive Apps, then Positron. Leave the form at its defaults and select Launch.
Expected: A session card appears under My Interactive Sessions. Within a few minutes it changes from Queued to Starting to Running, and a Connect to Positron button appears.

title: Test checklist
text:
2. Connect
Step: Select Connect to Positron.
Expected: Positron opens in a new browser tab. The address starts with /rnode/, followed by the node name and port. No sign-in page appears. The Welcome page or an empty editor is visible, and the status bar is at the bottom of the window.

title: Test checklist
text:
3. R console
Step: In the console pane, select the interpreter picker and choose an R version. If no R shows in the list, the node has no R on PATH. Then run:
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
mean(x)
Expected: The console prints [1] 2. The variables pane shows x.

title: Test checklist
text:
4. Python console
Step: In the interpreter picker, choose a Python version. Then run:
import sys
sys.version
Expected: The console prints the Python version. The variables pane shows no error. If Positron offers to install ipykernel, accept, and report the version it installs.

title: Test checklist
section: 5. Open a file in the working directory
text:
5. Open a file in the working directory
Step: In the explorer pane, open a file from the working directory, or create hello.R, type print("hello"), and save it with Ctrl+S.
Expected: The file opens in the editor and saves without an error. The file is visible from a shell on the cluster, in the same directory.

title: Test checklist
text:
6. Plots
Step: In the R console, run:
plot(1:10)
Expected: The plots pane shows a scatter plot of ten points.

title: Test checklist
text:
7. Data explorer
Step: In the R console, run:
View(mtcars)
Expected: A data explorer tab opens with 32 rows and 11 columns. Sorting a column by its header works.

title: Test checklist
text:
8. Session ends cleanly
Step: Close the Positron tab. In OOD, select Delete on the session card and confirm.
Expected: The session card disappears. squeue -u <user> on the cluster shows no job for the session. The session output directory keeps output.log, and the log ends without an error.

title: Test checklist
text:
9. A second session
Step: Launch the app again with the same user.
Expected: The session starts faster than the first one, and the extensions and settings from the first session are still there.

title: Test checklist
text:
Report
Send Posit the pass or fail result for each item, the Positron Server version from positron-server --version, the OOD version from Help, then About, and the session log for any failed item.
